title: kubelet is vulnerable to concurrent sort and can violate safety guarantees [v1.21.x]
body:
### What happened?

From time to time (with a very low chance), we see that some of our pods couldn't start, and failed with message like below:

```console
$ kubectl get pod goapp
NAME    READY   STATUS   RESTARTS   AGE
goapp   29/30   Error    9          118s
$ kubectl logs goapp -c p1251
2023/04/29 23:31:32 listen tcp :1251: bind: address already in use
``` 

And when I go to the host, I can see that there is already a container running for `p1251`, but kubelet tried to create another one regardless. (This violates the safety guarantee that kubelet should never try to launch two running instances for a single container spec in pod).

```console
$ docker ps -a | grep goapp_default | grep p1251
0207c985fa7c        731e2216ed4e             "/usr/local/bin/goap…"   19 seconds ago      Exited (1) 18 seconds ago                          k8s_p1251_goapp_default_c19bc8c4-6d62-4146-864e-b240015a0b36_6
c50f265a3b7c        731e2216ed4e             "/usr/local/bin/goap…"   3 minutes ago       Up 3 minutes
```

Given the container `p1251` already started 3 minutes ago, it is unexpected to see new containers coming up (though they can't because the specific port is already in-use). 


### What did you expect to happen?

I expect the pod should be Running without issues.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

I have a detailed step-by-step guide for this - https://github.com/zhouhaibing089/blog/issues/40. (To reproduce this successfully, it might be required to run multiple times).

To add the steps here, too:

1. Launch v1.21.14 cluster via minikube:

```console
$ minikube start --driver=virtualbox --cpus=4 --memory=8g --kubernetes-version=v1.21.14
```

2. Apply the pod specs from https://github.com/zhouhaibing089/goapp/tree/master/pods

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

[1]: https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C0BP8PW9G/p1682626134354939

By purely analysis, this is mostly like due to a concurrent sort in:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/57a3aa3f13699cf3db9c52d228c18db94fa81876/pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods.go#L1764

The function chain is like this:

`convertToAPIContainerStatuses` <- `convertStatusToAPIStatus` <- `generateAPIPodStatus`.

However, `generateAPIPodStatus` might be executed concurrently from:

1. `kubelet.syncPod` <- `kubelet.syncCh`

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/57a3aa3f13699cf3db9c52d228c18db94fa81876/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L1524

2. `kubelet.cleanUpContainersInPod` <- `kubelet.plegCh`.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/57a3aa3f13699cf3db9c52d228c18db94fa81876/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L2245
1.21 is EOL, you should report the issue with one of the supported versions https://kubernetes.io/releases/
Yeah, I'm aware of that, but I figured it out it might still be useful for others who still run v1.21.x. I don't expect a fix from community. But it would be great if people can find this.

I also think it is not a bad idea to reflect and try to learn from the past. For instance, there is no need to sort in `generateAPIPodStatus` at all (which the HEAD still does) becasue it is already sorted in podcache.

For people who wonder what a fix might look like, please take a look https://github.com/zhouhaibing089/kubernetes/commit/94e61f625d00d1d8c1414fd7d4a573425fa847b5.

title: Pods in terminal state are still counted as "used" count/pods quota
body:
### What happened?

According to https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/policy/resource-quotas/#object-count-quota:

| Resource Name | Description                                                                                                                                                     |
|---------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| pods          | The total number of Pods in a non-terminal state that can exist in the namespace. A pod is in a terminal state if .status.phase in (Failed, Succeeded) is true. |

Terminated pods are still counted as "used" count/pods quota. See the following section for repro steps.

### What did you expect to happen?

Terminal Pods shouldn't be counted as "used" count/pods quota.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

- Create a quota:
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: quota
spec:
  hard:
    count/pods: "8"
    limits.cpu: "4"
    limits.memory: 2000Gi
    requests.cpu: "4"
    requests.memory: 400Gi
```
- Create a Job with replicas=1
```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: countdown
spec:
  template:
    metadata:
      name: countdown
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: counter
        image: alpine
        resources:
          limits:
            cpu: "1"
            memory: 2Gi
          requests:
            cpu: "1"
            memory: 2Gi
        command:
         - "sh"
         - "-c"
         - "for i in 9 8 7 6 5 4 3 2 1 ; do echo $i ; done"
      restartPolicy: Never
```
- Check quota after the Job is completed
```console
⇒  k get job                                                                                                               (⎈|kind-kind:N/A)
NAME        COMPLETIONS   DURATION   AGE
countdown   1/1           7s         11s

⇒  k get quota                                                                                                             (⎈|kind-kind:N/A)
NAME    AGE   REQUEST                                                        LIMIT

pointsTests := []jsonpathTest{

title: client-go/kubectl rejects discovery API responses with charset encoding info
body:
We are using `client-go` (and `kubectl`) to interact with Kubernetes clusters behind a couple of proxy layers. One of these proxies completes the `Content-Type` headers to include character encoding details.

This was working fine until recently, when client-go/kubectl have started to fail when interacting with the discovery API. It seems that a recent change has made kubectl more restrictive of the content-type that it expects. I suspect that it is related to this commit: https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/commit/25d5761bfa0603c77cf5efefb14fd2e63a03a773

For example, this is an error from a kubectl command:
```
...
E0422 16:28:02.626222   86629 memcache.go:265] couldn't get current server API group list: Unknown discovery response content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8
I0422 16:28:02.626258   86629 cached_discovery.go:120] skipped caching discovery info due to Unknown discovery response content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8
I0422 16:28:02.626346   86629 shortcut.go:100] Error loading discovery information: Unknown discovery response content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8
...
```

We can of course try to fix it on our end, removing that charset information. However, it is a valid content-type and the way kubectl is handling the content-type there seems like it is relying on implementation details of kube-apiserver (that it does not add metadata to the content-type). I propose to fix this issue in `kubectl`, by properly parsing and handling the content-type.

title: Strategic Merge does not handle directives for empty slices.
body:
### What happened?

When performing a strategic merge for a slice of maps with `patchStrategy=merge`, directives in the patch slice are ignored if the original list is empty. Instead, the merged slice still contains the directives. This causes the patched object to fail subsequent validation since it has directives in a slice.

This behavior can be seen if one attempts to patch `ValidatingWebhookConfiguration.admissionregistration.k8s.io` specifically changes to the optional field [Webhooks](https://github.com/kubernetes/api/blob/master/admissionregistration/v1beta1/types.go#L93-L97).

If the original object has the following value
``` json
{
    "apiVersion": "admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1",
    "kind": "ValidatingWebhookConfiguration",
    "metadata": {
        "creationTimestamp": "2023-04-19T13:41:39Z",
        "generation": 2,
        "name": "base-validation",
        "resourceVersion": "200160",
        "uid": "70d47b26-ddba-430a-82d2-3fe7f8b4b840"
    }
}
```
And we attempt to do a strategic patch with the following information 
``` json
{
    "$setElementOrder/webhooks": [
        {
            "name": "new.foo.com"
        }
    ],
    "webhooks": [
        {
            "admissionReviewVersions": [
                "v1"
            ],
            "clientConfig": {
                "url": "https://foo.com"
            },
            "name": "new.foo.com",
            "sideEffects": "None"
        },
        {
            "$patch": "delete",
            "name": "foo.bar.com"
        }
    ]
}
```
The resulting object will look like the following JSON and fail validation.
``` json
{
    "apiVersion": "admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1",
    "kind": "ValidatingWebhookConfiguration",
    "metadata": {
        "creationTimestamp": "2023-04-19T13:41:39Z",
        "generation": 2,
        "name": "base-validation",
        "resourceVersion": "200160",
        "uid": "70d47b26-ddba-430a-82d2-3fe7f8b4b840"
    },
    "webhooks": [
        {
            "admissionReviewVersions": [
                "v1"
            ],
            "clientConfig": {
                "url": "https://foo.com"
            },
            "name": "new.foo.com",
            "sideEffects": "None"
        },
        {
            "$patch": "delete",
            "name": "foo.bar.com"
        }
    ]
}
```
Errors:
```
The ValidatingWebhookConfiguration "base-validation" is invalid: 
* webhooks[1].sideEffects: Required value: must specify one of None, NoneOnDryRun
* webhooks[1].clientConfig: Required value: exactly one of url or service is required
* webhooks[1].admissionReviewVersions: Required value: must specify one of v1, v1beta1
```


### What did you expect to happen?

Strategic merge always handles any directives in the patch.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

## Repo steps with kubectl
1. Apply the following webhook configuration `kubectl apply`
    ``` yaml
    apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
    kind: ValidatingWebhookConfiguration
    metadata:
      name: base-validation
    webhooks:
      - name: foo.bar.com
        admissionReviewVersions:
          - "v1"
        clientConfig:
          url: https://foo.com
        sideEffects: None
    ```
2. Edit the newly created webhook and remove the Webhooks list. `kubectl edit validatingwebhookconfiguration base-validation`

3. Attempt to apply the following webhook configuration with `kubectl apply`
      ``` yaml
      apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
      kind: ValidatingWebhookConfiguration
      metadata:
        name: base-validation
      webhooks:
        - name: new.foo.com
          admissionReviewVersions:
            - "v1"
          clientConfig:
            url: https://foo.com
          sideEffects: None
    ```

Notice that the request fails with the following errors
```
The ValidatingWebhookConfiguration "base-validation" is invalid: 
* webhooks[1].sideEffects: Required value: must specify one of None, NoneOnDryRun
* webhooks[1].clientConfig: Required value: exactly one of url or service is required
* webhooks[1].admissionReviewVersions: Required value: must specify one of v1, v1beta1
```

### Anything else we need to know?

The logic causing this behavior for the example can be seen here in [apimachinery](https://github.com/kubernetes/apimachinery/blob/master/pkg/util/strategicpatch/patch.go#L1179-L1194)
In this code, we see that if the original value was not found, we blindly assign the `patchFieldValue`

nodes.title: Fix Strategic Merge merging leaving patch directives in objects when field doesn't exist
nodes.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

When Strategic Merge Patch is merging a value against a non-existent field, it has logic to simply take the patch value. This causes problems when the patch value includes a nested directive which is then included in the saved object.

This PR attempts to fix this by finding all the locations where the patch value is taken and instead of simply taking the value, changes the logic to continue recursion into patch value to remove directives.

body:
### What happened?

After updating to Kubernetes 1.27.1 some containers using `k8s.io/api v0.26.1` are crashing because of SIGSEGV (Segmentation Violation) and they can no longer communicate with the cluster. Originally, this also occurred with my local kubectl installation of version 1.26.3, but now it seems to be working again.

Everything seemed to work fine until I updated the very last node in the cluster from 1.26.3 to 1.27.1. So the first 5 nodes had no problems, even with the containers that are now failing.

### What did you expect to happen?

I expect the containers to work just as they were before, as this version difference should be covered by the [Kubernetes version skew policy](https://kubernetes.io/releases/version-skew-policy/). So no segmentation violation should happen and the API access should be compatible.

1. Deploy a Kubernetes cluster in version 1.27.1

title: OpenAPI spec fetching ignores apiserver URL path
body:
### What happened?

This was originally reported in https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/issues/407161. GitLab Agent for Kubernetes, apart from other things, is a Kubernetes API reverse proxy. Users recently started getting errors when using it with kubectl v1.27.x.

Users' CI jobs get a generated kubectl-compatible config file, where server URL has a path component. For GitLab.com the address is `https://kas.gitlab.com/k8s-proxy/`. Looks like kubectl v1.27.x ignores the path component for some OpenAPI requests - here is an output for a `kubectl apply` run:

### What did you expect to happen?

Command should work normally.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

nodes.title: Use absolute path instead requestURI in openapiv3 discovery
nodes.body:
#### What type of PR is this?
/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:
Currently, openapiv3 discovery uses requestURI to discover resources. However, that does not work when the rest endpoint contains prefixes (e.g. `http://localhost/test-endpoint/`).
Because requestURI overwrites prefixes also in rest endpoint (e.g. `http://localhost/openapiv3/apis/apps/v1`).

Since `absPath` keeps the prefixes in the rest endpoint, this PR changes to absPath instead requestURI(e.g. `http://localhost/test-endpoint/openapiv3/apis/apps/v1`).

#### Which issue(s) this PR fixes:
Fixes #117463

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?
```release-note
Fixes a 1.26 regression in kubectl and client-go discovery when configured with a server URL other than the root of a server.
```

/kind api-change
/kind deprecation
/kind failing-test
/kind flake
/kind regression
-->

/kind bug 

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

The `providerID` is used by the cloud-provider code to correlate the Node to the underlying cloud instance. The service controller in the KCCM does not define the provider ID as a predicate for syncing nodes, hence nodes can be passed to the cloud-provider code with a missing provider ID. Should the cloud-provider not handle the missing provider ID as an error, and instead silently fail: then the load balancers won't be re-synced with the node in question. Moreover: the service controller does not sync the assignment of the providerID on the Node object 
    
This PR adds the provider ID as a predicate for syncing the node. As such we are sure the cloud provider won't error at any time because of this missing attribute, and we always re-sync the node once it gets the provider ID set.  

This was overlooked in #109706 because the providerID was never explicitly defined in the service controller for syncing nodes, it was indirectly covered by the fact that the service controller always synced nodes on the Ready condition...which comes after the setting of the providerID on the Node object. Also, others clouds might have other mechanisms for retrieving the instance besides solely relying on the providerID.

title: Remove unnecessary kube::golang::verify_go_version from update-mocks.sh
body:
### What happened? **kube::golang::verify_go_version** is the first function we execute from kube::golang::setup_env. See update-mocks.sh ``` trap cleanup EXIT kube::golang::verify_go_version kube::golang::setup_env echo 'installing mockgen' pushd "${KUBE_ROOT}/hack/tools" >/dev/null go install github.com/golang/mock/mockgen ``` ``` % grep -rn -B1 -A1 "kube::golang::verify_go_version" /Users/marthinal/go/src/k8s.io/kubernetes/hack/lib/golang.sh /Users/marthinal/go/src/k8s.io/kubernetes/hack/update-mocks.sh --color /Users/marthinal/go/src/k8s.io/kubernetes/hack/lib/golang.sh-464-# env-var FORCE_HOST_GO set to a non-empty value uses the go version in the $PATH and skips ensuring $GO_VERSION is used /Users/marthinal/go/src/k8s.io/kubernetes/hack/lib/golang.sh:465:kube::golang::verify_go_version() { /Users/marthinal/go/src/k8s.io/kubernetes/hack/lib/golang.sh-466- # default GO_VERSION to content of .go-version -- /Users/marthinal/go/src/k8s.io/kubernetes/hack/lib/golang.sh-508-kube::golang::setup_env() { /Users/marthinal/go/src/k8s.io/kubernetes/hack/lib/golang.sh:509: kube::golang::verify_go_version /Users/marthinal/go/src/k8s.io/kubernetes/hack/lib/golang.sh-510- -- /Users/marthinal/go/src/k8s.io/kubernetes/hack/update-mocks.sh-38- /Users/marthinal/go/src/k8s.io/kubernetes/hack/update-mocks.sh:39:kube::golang::verify_go_version /Users/marthinal/go/src/k8s.io/kubernetes/hack/update-mocks.sh-40-kube::golang::setup_env ``` We execute kube::golang::verify_go_version then kube::golang::setup_env and then kube::golang::verify_go_version again from kube::golang::setup_env I found this issue while working on #117272 ### What did you expect to happen? Do not execute kube::golang::verify_go_version twice. ### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)? ### What happened?

I tried setting up Kubernetes following the Getting Started guide on creating a cluster with kubeadm.

`kubeadm init` ran through without issues, but the control plane services are stuck in some kind of restart loop, which I could not figure out the reason for. `kubectl` is functional only intermittently (at the times when etcd and apiserver are both up)

```
$ kubectl get pods --all-namespaces

I had this same issue, and it turned out `SystemdCgroup` wasn't getting set properly in `/etc/containerd/config.toml`. I was only using the configuration in the [container runtime installation docs](https://kubernetes.io/docs/setup/production-environment/container-runtimes/#containerd-systemd); I didn't have the rest of the config file. After generating a baseline config with `containerd config default > /etc/containerd/config.toml` and editing the `SystemdCgroup` setting there, the problem went away.

(The docs mention this in a note, but mostly qualifies it as something to try if you used a distro package, which I didn't do, so I had skipped over it.)

@liggitt thank you so much for the quick turnaround. When 1.27.1 gets released we'll let Flux users know they can safely upgrade.

Location:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f5095bf34dba15c702b4618bcd24aae6fc2f47b2/staging/src/k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/debug/debug.go#L630-L637

title: `volume.SetVolumeOwnership()` always fails when called for wrapped volume
body:
### What happened?

Every time `volume.SetVolumeOwnership(ed)` from `empty_dir.go` is called for a projected volume, it fails with "no such file or directory" error.

The problem comes from the fact that `SetVolumeOwnership()` always calculates the root dir for ownership changes as `mounter.GetPath()` while projected.go explicitly passes another dir as the first arg of `SetUpAt()` call:
```
	if err := wrapped.SetUpAt(dir, mounterArgs); err != nil {
		return err
	}
```
(see https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/96306f144a3c917a97fe27c9ad5dd89e4213f741/pkg/volume/projected/projected.go#L203)

### What did you expect to happen?

`volume.SetVolumeOwnership()` must succeed when a projected volume is created.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Print return value of `volume.SetVolumeOwnership()` when called from `empty_dir.go`:
```
diff --git a/pkg/volume/emptydir/empty_dir.go b/pkg/volume/emptydir/empty_dir.go
index 9ad981c54bd..ce3f7d330fe 100644
--- a/pkg/volume/emptydir/empty_dir.go
+++ b/pkg/volume/emptydir/empty_dir.go
@@ -280,7 +280,10 @@ func (ed *emptyDir) SetUpAt(dir string, mounterArgs volume.MounterArgs) error {
                err = fmt.Errorf("unknown storage medium %q", ed.medium)
        }
 
-       volume.SetVolumeOwnership(ed, mounterArgs.FsGroup, nil /*fsGroupChangePolicy*/, volumeutil.FSGroupCompleteHook(ed.plugin, nil))
+       e := volume.SetVolumeOwnership(ed, mounterArgs.FsGroup, nil /*fsGroupChangePolicy*/, volumeutil.FSGroupCompleteHook(ed.plugin, nil))
+       if e != nil {
+               klog.Infof("ZZZ: SetVolumeOwnership() returned error: %v (dir: %v; ed.GetPath(): %v)", e, dir, ed.GetPath())
+       }
 
        // If setting up the quota fails, just log a message but don't actually error out.
        // We'll use the old du mechanism in this case, at least until we support
```

Start an arbitrary pod, then look at kubelet logs:
```
$ kubectl apply -f fedora.yaml

$ grep ZZZ /tmp/kubelet.log

```

nodes.title: Fix directory mismatch for `volume.SetVolumeOwnership()`
nodes.body:
In most cases `dir` arg of `SetUpAt()` method of `volume.Mounter` interface is the same as `mounter.GetPath()` because we usually call `SetUpAt()` from `SetUp()` like this:
```
func (ed *emptyDir) SetUp(mounterArgs volume.MounterArgs) error {
	return ed.SetUpAt(ed.GetPath(), mounterArgs)
}
```
(this example is from `volume/emptydir/empty_dir.go`, but there are plenty other examples like that in `volume/*`)

However, there is currently one exception. This is from `volume/projected/projected.go`:
```
	if err := wrapped.SetUpAt(dir, mounterArgs); err != nil {
		return err
	}
```
(see https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/96306f144a3c917a97fe27c9ad5dd89e4213f741/pkg/volume/projected/projected.go#L203)

In this case `dir` is not equal to `wrapped.GetPath()` and `volume.SetVolumeOwnership()` fails when called from `SetUpAt()` of wrapped volume:
```
lstat /var/lib/kubelet/pods/a2f6e58f-7edf-4c48-a97c-ef1b8fd3caf6/volumes/kubernetes.io~empty-dir/wrapped_kube-api-access-knvkv: no such file or directory
```

To fix the issue let's pass `dir` arg to `volume.SetVolumeOwnership()` explicitly, and use it instead of `mounter.GetPath()`.

cc @smarterclayton @bobbypage @mimowo this might a regression in 1.27.0-rc.0 with this PR #115331
Even if it is, it sounds like a bug in daemonset instead. Why wouldn't it replace pods that are terminated? It can probably be reproduced in integration.

I think there might be something with the fact that Calico terminates with exit code '0', so it feels like a "successful" run. Still such pod should be restarted, so I'm not sure why it doesn't get restarted after a reboot.

> @smira let me ask to get more details about reproducing this locally. Are you running this on Kind? How do you trigger the the restarts? Can you share mode details on the node configuration, such as the graceful shutdown period?

Let me try to build a reproduce instruction in the next comment.
@mimowo I also have complete output of `kubectl get` under the details in the issue itself.

> I think there might be something with the fact that Calico terminates with exit code '0', so it feels like a "successful" run.

The daemonset controller should still recreate the pod in that scenario.

/sig apps

The reproducer is to follow the [Talos QEMU guide](https://www.talos.dev/v1.4/talos-guides/install/local-platforms/qemu/), but it should be same under any Talos platforms except Docker (which doesn't have a graceful node shutdown, and any kind of shutdown).

I verified it with the assets from the latest [1.4.0-alpha.4 release](https://github.com/siderolabs/talos/releases/tag/v1.4.0-alpha.4).

The smallest I can reproduce it with is 1+1 cluster, but it looks same way e.g. in 3+2 cluster:

```
sudo -E talosctl cluster create --provisioner=qemu --controlplanes 1 --workers 1 --custom-cni-url=https://raw.githubusercontent.com/projectcalico/calico/v3.25.0/manifests/calico.yaml
```

Once the cluster is up, all the pods are running & healthy (`kubectl get pods -A -o wide`). If I issue a reboot of the worker node with `talosctl -n 10.5.0.3 reboot`, with `watch -n 2 kubectl get pods -A -o wide` shows that `calico-node` pod on the worker node quickly enters `Completed` state, and never recovers.

At the same time I don't quite understand what is exactly wrong, as if I just do a daemonset with `sleep 10` command, the pod also enters `Completed` state, but it gets quickly restarted by the `kubelet` via `CrashLoopBackOff` transition.
I can also send kubelet logs, and anything else which might be helpful to debug the issue, I'm also open to do a debug session with screen sharing.

> At the same time I don't quite understand what is exactly wrong, as if I just do a daemonset with `sleep 10` command, the pod also enters `Completed` state, but it gets quickly restarted by the `kubelet` via `CrashLoopBackOff` transition.

This is because of `restartPolicy: Always`. The pod doesn't reach the `Succeeded` phase in this case. The kubelet just recreates the containers. However, when a pod is actually marked as "Succeeded" then kubelet would stop looking at it.

However, it should be the responsibility of the daemonset controller to recreate a pod.

Following the sig-apps advise opened the PR (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/117073) with an integration test for DaemonSet. 

It passes for Failed pods, but fails for Succeeded. In other words, the succeeded pods are not restarted. I'm yet to investigate (probably tomorrow) why this is so, but it seems like a bug. In the meanwhile some expertise about DaemonSets would be helpful.

Thanks for reporting this. I suppose this might be related to the fact that `restartAlways` pods (created by daemonset) can now be marked as [terminal phase](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d89d5ab2680bc74fe4487ad71e514f4e0812d9ce/pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods.go#L1463-L1486) in v1.27.

When graceful node shutdown happens, we terminate the pod with `killPodNow`:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d89d5ab2680bc74fe4487ad71e514f4e0812d9ce/pkg/kubelet/nodeshutdown/nodeshutdown_manager_linux.go#L377

which will trigger kubelet to terminate the pod in pod worker (`syncTerminatingPod/syncTerminatedPod`) and eventually I assume set a terminal phase on the pod. We should verify if that is what is happening here.

In either case, +1 on comment that I would expect that daemonset controller should recreate a pod if it is marked completed.

I will note that the intent for graceful shutdown was always that pods could be marked Succeeded (vs just Failed), since the pod is indeed terminal.  It's likely that this was previously racy (no guarantee succeeded made it to the apiserver) and #115331 fixed that.

However, outside of graceful shutdown this should never occur - do we have any evidence a RestartAlways pod went succeeded in that case (wasn't clear from the thread)?  That would be a serious bug.

> However, outside of graceful shutdown this should never occur - do we have any evidence a RestartAlways pod went succeeded in that case (wasn't clear from the thread)? That would be a serious bug.

I think Succeeded would also be possible in other scenarios, like deletion (deletionTimestamp!=nil). This I've tested for Job pods, but I think DS pods would behave the same. 

Except for deletion I think the behavior is limited to graceful node shutdown, which invokes the kill function, but respects the Succeeded phase: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/nodeshutdown/nodeshutdown_manager_linux.go#L377-L381. Other uses of the kill function unconditionally set Failed, such as the eviction manager: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/eviction/eviction_manager.go#L586.

EDIT: oh, actually for Jobs we don't use restartPolicy=Always, but still deleted pods with  restartPolicy=Always may still terminate with Succeeded phase as shown in this test: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d89d5ab2680bc74fe4487ad71e514f4e0812d9ce/test/e2e_node/deleted_pods_test.go#L142
Deletion with RestartAlways is ok, because the pod goes away reasonably fast (but we are adding latency in 1.27 to that path) as you note.

No, 1 az has no nodes without enough free cpu capacity while the others have some.
The nodes in all azs have enough memory/cpu to fit the pod if they were empty/

```
Node:                 <none>
Status:               Pending
...
Topology Spread Constraints:  topology.kubernetes.io/zone:DoNotSchedule when max skew 1 is exceeded for selector pod-template-hash=69fb6f5469,role=donotschedule
...
  Warning  FailedScheduling  46s   default-scheduler  0/17 nodes are available: 1 Insufficient cpu, 1 node(s) had untolerated taint {node.kubernetes.io/unschedulable: }, 10 node(s) had untolerated taint {ownedby: compute}, 11 node(s) didn't match pod topology spread constraints, 3 node(s) had untolerated taint {node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane: true}, 6 node(s) were unschedulable. preemption: not eligible due to preemptionPolicy=Never.
```

Ah, ok, I misunderstood the situation. Thanks for sharing the detail.
Then, the answer is that everything is working expectedly from the scheduler's PoV.

The scheduler basically schedules pending Pods one by one. It doesn't take any other pending Pods into consideration during scheduling.

So, in your scenario, 
1. the scheduler scheduled the first two Pods to different zone's Nodes.
2. the scheduler wanted to schedule the next one to the third zone, but Pods couldn't go due to insufficient resources.
3. All other Pods got unschedulable in the same reason.
4. As a result, 2 went to Nodes, and other couldn't go anywhere.

Yeah, that sounds about right.
So a possible fix would be to make the scheduler look at pending pods too.

Current behavior is bad when 1 az is in trouble and then suddenly the whole app is down, only semi-fix I found so far was to cordon the whole AZ and then use "nodeTaintsPolicy: Honor", but that means manual effort and another restart for all pods.

I wouldn't say the current behavior is wrong.
Because if it goes as your expectation (`3/9 being pending in the bad AZ`), it obviously violates the `maxSkew`.

> Current behavior is bad when 1 az is in trouble and then suddenly the whole app is down

But, this is true. If one az has trouble, that affects the scheduling on other zones as well.
So, probably, what we want to have is something like https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/105977.

Yeah that sounds good!

On Fri, Mar 31, 2023 at 7:09 PM Kensei Nakada ***@***.***>
wrote:

> Current behavior is bad when 1 az is in trouble and then suddenly the
> whole app is down
>
> But, this is true. If one az has trouble, that affects the scheduling on
> other zones as well.
> So, probably, what we want to have is #105977
> <https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/105977>.
>
> —
> Reply to this email directly, view it on GitHub
> <https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/116978#issuecomment-1492793726>,
> or unsubscribe
> <https://github.com/notifications/unsubscribe-auth/AAACYZ6JW2ZSWSEFBSZKQVTW66E7LANCNFSM6AAAAAAWLMUBIE>
> .
> You are receiving this because you were mentioned.Message ID:
> ***@***.***>
>

> Because if it goes as your expectation (3/9 being pending in the bad AZ), it obviously violates the maxSkew.

I think the behaviour may be correct in the sense that it is what is documented but I think it would be much more useful to consider Pending pods in the calculation. This is because I think the expectation when someone is setting maxSkew to 1 with replicas 9 is that if one of three AZ is down is that they would still have 6 pods running not that they would be limited to only 2 pods.

I was talking about the current documented behavior, Yes. And, as the past me mentioned, https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/105977 is necessary if we want the scheduler to behave like your thought. (which I've been hoping to implement for a long time, but pending due to SIG-Autoscaling's bandwidth for reviewing KEP.)

> if one of three AZ is down is that they would still have 6 pods running not that they would be limited to only 2 pods.

Actually, "one of three AZ is down" is a bit different from what I was assuming for this issue, which defined the situation like "1 of the AZs have insufficient capacity".

In your case, if all nodes within one AZ facing issue have taints properly, you can just use `nodeTaintsPolicy: Honor` and then your scheduler should ignore all nodes in the dead AZ at the spreading calculation, and schedule all your pods into two healthy AZs evenly.

I think my point was more that I think it still makes sense to schedule pods to an AZ even "maxSkew" might be exceeded provided that after all the Pending pods are scheduled the skew is less than maxSkew. It seems relatively easy to compute just check `<pods in AZ + 1> < <max Skew>  + <total pods> / <domains>`. I agree that would be a change but I don't understand how anyone could depend on the previous behaviour.

In our case I think it makes sense to use three StatefulSets because that also solves some edge cases around scaling as because of a PVC we can't "move" pods between AZs.

First, as you mentioned, we cannot break this existing behavior in the first place. We'd need an API so that people can opt-in the behavior only if they want, and otherwise keep the current behavior. 

Second, from a technical perspective, the scheduler doesn't know which pods belong to the same group. It just schedules pods one by one and don't consider other pending pods.

Let's say pod-a has this constraint:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: pod-a
  labels:
    app: awesome-app
spec:
...
          topologySpreadConstraints:
            - labelSelector:
                matchLabels:
                  app: awesome-app
              maxSkew: 1
              topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
              whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
```

Then, if we want to compute like your formula, how would it get `<total pods>`? It's not correct to assume pods with `app: awesome-app` label as `<total pods>` because maybe not all pods with the label have the constraint. 

And, third, from the behavior perspective, why do we still want to keep 2 pods pending (in your scenario)? I know the current behavior is worse because it only allows only 2 pods to be scheduled, while keeping 7 pods pending. 
But, I believe the ideal behavior, in general, is to just spread pods evenly on _available_ AZs for reliability. For example, people just want to keep pods spread across all available AZs so that the service can be reliable even when one AZ is dead. And then, when one AZ is actually dead, they probably wouldn't want to keep pods in one AZ pending, but they would expect them to be scheduled on other AZs instead of a dead AZ so that the service gets a full replicas coming back soon even after one AZ's issue.
That's why I'm saying let's wait for https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/105977 (or use `nodeTaintsPolicy`, although that involves the troublesomeness of putting taints onto all nodes in the dead AZ). It's simpler and more aligned with that expectation; people define their pods can be fallback to other AZs in such cases. In your scenario, if one AZ is dead, all pods would go to two alive AZs evenly, not keeping two pods pending.

Also, sidenote though, Pod Topology Spread is already one of the slowest in-tree plugins. So, for that reason as well, we don't want to put additional calculations basically in it.

That makes sense I think the part I wasn't aware of was that the plugin is only aware of the scheduled pods.

I think there's cases with Volumes that are tied to an AZ where you wouldn't want to fallback to different zones and without the Descheduler it would mean that it still recover after. I do concede though it doesn't look really practical to change this though and there are other ways to solve the issue.

nodes.body:
#### What type of PR is this?
/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

this check needs to go after any mutations. After the mutating admission chain, rest.BeforeUpdate (which is responsible for reverting updates to immutable timestamp fields, among other things.) is called in the store.Update function. This makes it possible for an object to be written to etcd with only a change to its managed fields timestamp. 

This PR moves the check for these noop writes deeper in the handler chain, to the after the last point the object is modified.

title: Memory leak in kubelet volume_manager populator processedPods
body:
### What happened?

If a pod is created and then deleted an entry in processedPods map remains forever (sometimes, it's racy).

The problem comes from the fact that `podWorker` calls volume_manager `WaitForUnmount()` asynchronously. If the last call happens after populator cleaned up resources, an entry is added to processedPods and will never be seen.

### What did you expect to happen?

An entry in processedPods map must be deleted if pod doesn't exist and pod runtime should removed according to `dswp.podStateProvider`.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

To verify that the issue really exists I applaied a simple [patch](https://github.com/jsafrane/kubernetes/commit/40ffc8e62836244ea6cffde8b9dff2c402d058c5) printing resources in `processedPods` map. Here is a reproducer:

1. Start brand-new fresh k8s cluster with `hack/local-up-cluster.sh`
2. Check entries in `processedPods`:
```
I0321 15:03:42.131049    2149 desired_state_of_world_populator.go:264] JSAF: processed pod ac109c78-ce77-4426-9421-53fbcfe2175b: true
I0321 15:03:43.131815    2149 desired_state_of_world_populator.go:262] JSAF: processed pods size: 1
```
3. Create a pod, check its uid:
```
$ k get po fdroot -o yaml |grep uid
  uid: a0158a6e-3b23-4a68-a50b-5d44e0fc009a
```
4. Verify that this uid is accurately reported:
```
I0321 15:05:06.193326    2149 desired_state_of_world_populator.go:262] JSAF: processed pods size: 2
I0321 15:05:06.193412    2149 desired_state_of_world_populator.go:264] JSAF: processed pod ac109c78-ce77-4426-9421-53fbcfe2175b: true
I0321 15:05:06.193434    2149 desired_state_of_world_populator.go:264] JSAF: processed pod a0158a6e-3b23-4a68-a50b-5d44e0fc009a: true
```
5. Delete the pod, wait for a few mins, check for `processedPods` again:
```
I0321 15:48:29.113233    2149 desired_state_of_world_populator.go:262] JSAF: processed pods size: 3
I0321 15:48:29.113252    2149 desired_state_of_world_populator.go:264] JSAF: processed pod ac109c78-ce77-4426-9421-53fbcfe2175b: true
I0321 15:48:29.113259    2149 desired_state_of_world_populator.go:264] JSAF: processed pod a0158a6e-3b23-4a68-a50b-5d44e0fc009a: false
I0321 15:48:29.113262    2149 desired_state_of_world_populator.go:264] JSAF: processed pod 213bcdcb-c9e7-4d96-af41-353d651cbd86: true
```

The entry `a0158a6e-3b23-4a68-a50b-5d44e0fc009a: false` will be kept forever because kubelet doesn't know anything about this pod anymore:
```
$ k get pods --all-namespaces -o yaml |grep "a0158a6e-3b23-4a68-a50b-5d44e0fc009a"
$
```
so no more events will ever come to populater for this uid, and the loop in `findAndRemoveDeletedPods()` won't find it because it was already deleted from `dswp.desiredStateOfWorld`.

### Anything else we need to know?

n/a

/sig node
FYI @bobbypage @smarterclayton

/triage accepted

since it's a new error, it is a regression. So adding a corresponding priority

/priority important-soon
@bobbypage are you working on this? Should I assign bug to you?

Yes, I'm taking a look at this.

/assign

/cc

https://storage.googleapis.com/k8s-triage/index.html?text=kubelet_working_pods#019385d67e058439e83e
This is a metrics only error (we don’t report a fraction of metrics) and has no functional impact.

That makes sense, but is it expected that this is a valid state in first place? `State:sync Orphan:false HasConfig:false Static:false`. 

My assumption was that if static is false, (i.e. API pod) then we should have a config?

I took a closer look at the logs, it seems that this is happening when we enter `HandlePodCleanups` while a static pod is being synced which has UID reuse and another pod which has the same full name did not terminate yet. 

In this case, we block the static pod from starting i.e. (`canStart`) returns false:
 https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/c3e7eca7fd38454200819b60e58144d5727f1bbc/pkg/kubelet/pod_workers.go#L1007-L1019. 

Because the pod can't start, we don't set `startedAt`: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/c3e7eca7fd38454200819b60e58144d5727f1bbc/pkg/kubelet/pod_workers.go#L1168-L1169

which means that when we log metrics there is no `activeUpdate` set and thus `HasConfig` or `Static` are both defaulted to false:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/c3e7eca7fd38454200819b60e58144d5727f1bbc/pkg/kubelet/pod_workers.go#L1548-L1551

nodes.title: kubelet: Ensure pods that have not started track a pendingUpdate
nodes.body:
A pod that cannot be started yet (due to static pod fullname
exclusion when UIDs are reused) must be accounted for in the
pod worker since it is considered to have been admitted and will
eventually start.

Due to a bug we accidentally cleared pendingUpdate for pods that
cannot start yet which means we can't report the right metric to
users in kubelet_working_pods and in theory we might fail to start
the pod in the future (although we currently have not observed
that in tests that should catch such an error). Describe, implement,
and test the invariant that when startPodSync returns in every path
that either activeUpdate OR pendingUpdate is set on the status, but
never both, and is only nil when the pod can never start.

This bug was detected by a "programmer error" assertion we added
on metrics that were not being reported, suggesting that we should
be more aggressive on using log assertions and automating detection
in tests.

Fixed #116715 

/kind bug
/sig node
/priority important-soon

In theory this is a pretty significant bug in static pods and should be part of 1.27 - but we don't have evidence yet that it's failing, in which case this can wait for 1.28 as a fix for the metrics.

```release-note
Static pods were taking extra time to be restarted after being updated.  Static pods that are waiting to restart were not correctly counted in `kubelet_working_pods`.

title: Edge case - job pods nearing completion being evicted even though protected by PodDisruptionBudget
body:
### What happened?

I believe I've come across an edge case in evictions which can cause job pods to be evicted and replaced even though they complete without error.

Here's the scenario:

- Create a job with `completions` and `parallelism` both set to 3.
- Add a PodDisruptionBudget in place for this job's pods, with `minAvailable` set to 3.
- All three pods are created and run successfully without crashing or hitting an `activeDeadlineSeconds` deadline.
- Just around the time the pods are about to complete their work and move from `Running` to `Completed`, one of them is selected for eviction by the [Descheduler](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/descheduler)
- The eviction is successful, and results in a replacement pod being created.

In terms of frequency, we don't see this problem often - perhaps a couple of times over hundreds of jobs - but it is a persistent issue that we've seen over months.

### What did you expect to happen?

I would expect a replacement pod not to have been created, as all three pods appear to have completed successfully, and the PodDisruptionBudget should protect them from a descheduler-triggered eviction.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

I've come up with a crude reproducible testcase that shows the problem roughly 4 out of 5 times against a [kind](https://kind.sigs.k8s.io) cluster. It's automated in the shell script below. Obviously I don't have the descheduler running in that kind cluster, so I have a repeated loop of eviction attempts (via the [kubectl-evict plugin](https://github.com/ueokande/kubectl-evict)) which I think exhibits the same behaviour as a descheduler-initiated eviction attempt happening at the appropriate point to trigger to issue.

```
#!/usr/bin/env bash

kubectl --context kind create ns troubleshooting
kubectl --context kind -n troubleshooting delete job/my-test-job pdb/my-test-job-pdb

cat << EOF | kubectl --context kind -n troubleshooting apply -f -
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: my-test-job
spec:
  completions: 3
  parallelism: 3
  backoffLimit: 0
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: my-test-job
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: alpine
          image: alpine:3.14
          command: ["sleep", "1m"]
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 0m
              memory: 16Mi
            limits:
              memory: 16Mi
      restartPolicy: Never
---
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: my-test-job-pdb
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: my-test-job
  minAvailable: 3
EOF

# Wait about a minute for the job to complete
echo "Waiting for job to near completion"
sleep 60

# Pick a pod to evict
podToEvict=$(kubectl --context kind -n troubleshooting get pods | tail -n1 | awk '{ print $1 }')
echo "Will evict $podToEvict"

# Repeatedly try to evict in an attempt to hit the window of the problem
while true; do
  kubectl evict --context kind -n troubleshooting pod/$podToEvict
  result=$?
  if [[ "$result" = "0" ]]; then
    exit
  fi
done
```

### Anything else we need to know?

title: Last apiserver to shutdown doesn't remove its IP from k8s svc endpoints
body:
### What happened?

As part of the apiserver's pre-shutdown sequence, we stop the lease-controller from renewing the apiserver's etcd lease anymore and delete the lease:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/125e38c0872521bec49351415cc9fb624b046659/pkg/controlplane/controller.go#L211-L215

As part of the `RemoveEndpoints` call we expect that after the lease is deleted, the apiserver's IP is also removed from the k8s service endpoints object:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/125e38c0872521bec49351415cc9fb624b046659/pkg/controlplane/reconcilers/lease.go#L315-L321

However, `doReconcile` isn't removing the IP if it's the last remaining one:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/125e38c0872521bec49351415cc9fb624b046659/pkg/controlplane/reconcilers/lease.go#L210-L215

The comment there is assuming that `doReconcile` is always called after renewing the lease, which is incorrect since it can also be called as part of the shutdown workflow.

### What did you expect to happen?

The IP of the apiserver (even though it's the last one remaining) should be removed from k8s svc endpoints on shutdown.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Shutdown the last apiserver of the cluster and you'll see logs like this:

```
I1031 17:34:49.517758      12 controller.go:181] Shutting down kubernetes service endpoint reconciler
E1031 17:34:49.534880      12 controller.go:184] no master IPs were listed in storage, refusing to erase all endpoints for the kubernetes service
```

And the audit logs also confirm that the IP isn't removed from k8s endpoints object.

### Anything else we need to know?

Why is the above an issue?

If the IP isn't removed from the k8s endpoints object, clients (using in-cluster API mode) will try to continue talking/connecting to that instance even after the apiserver is dead. There are at least two issues with this:
- Causes confusing `i/o timeout` and `connection refused` errors for clients, instead of a cleaner `no route to host` error
- If the apiserver pod is restarted by kubelet (let's say due to healthcheck failure), clients may start talking to it prematurely even without healthz/readyz passing. This is not a recommended behavior ([xref](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/using-api/health-checks/)) as a bunch post-startup hooks like informer sync, internal controllers, etc may not have initialized yet

/sig api-machinery

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/8decaf3ae7f410ab3f3774f3895b9f3124b8a4c6/pkg/controlplane/reconcilers/lease.go#L146-L151

interesting, that bool is called under lock

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/8decaf3ae7f410ab3f3774f3895b9f3124b8a4c6/pkg/controlplane/reconcilers/lease.go#L169-L184

and the reconcile process is locked, so it that changes during the reconcile process the internal loop will never see it.
If that changes before the process the internal loop is not going to be executed.

@czybjtu let's try to remove that lock and bool with an atomic.bool  and improve the shutdown process, we should not bail out soon if we want to update the lease ... send a PR with these things and we'll take it from there
I found that `ReconcileEndpoints` and `StopReconciling` function are called in different goroutines. If we remove the lock, will it cause a race condition problem?

> I found that `ReconcileEndpoints` and `StopReconciling` function are called in different goroutines.

If we remove the lock, these two functions may call the `doReconcile` function at the same time, which could lead to unexpected results. Therefore, for safety reasons, I do not recommend using them without locks.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/8decaf3ae7f410ab3f3774f3895b9f3124b8a4c6/pkg/controlplane/reconcilers/lease.go#L252-L258

Correct me if I'm wrong.

remove the lock and replace the bool by `atomic.Bool`

EDIT

sorry, I misunderstood the comment, let me check it, good catch

Actually, leaseEndpointReconciler never deletes endpoints. It deletes lease resources. So it's not useful when we do like this.
```diff
 func (r *leaseEndpointReconciler) doReconcile(serviceName string, endpointPorts []corev1.EndpointPort, reconcilePorts bool) error {
        e, err := r.epAdapter.Get(corev1.NamespaceDefault, serviceName, metav1.GetOptions{})
        shouldCreate := false
@@ -192,6 +190,11 @@ func (r *leaseEndpointReconciler) doReconcile(serviceName string, endpointPorts
                        return err
                }
 
+               // there are no endpoints and we should stop reconciling
+               if r.stopReconcilingCalled.Load() {
+                       return nil
+               }
+
```
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/742316ee2136b24b9edb0bb0d5bf69a6bad6f364/pkg/controlplane/reconcilers/lease.go#L316

The execution order of these two gorotinues is completely unpredictable. So I don't think we could use `atomic.Bool` instead of lock by add  some logic like`if r.stopReconcilingCalled.Load() { return ...}`

In other words, even if the `StopReconciling `  function deletes the endpoint, `ReconcileEndpoints` function may still add it back.

> If the apiserver is the last one, RemoveEndpoints first deletes the lease and calls doReconcile.
> doReconcile doesn't update the Endpoints to indicate "there are no IPs", because of

Both ReconcileEndpoints and RemoveEndpoints will call `doReconcile`.  Since they are executed in two separate goroutines, the order in which they execute the `doReconcile` function is unknown.  

I think RemoveEndpoints could do what we expected. 

`doReconcile` which called by `ReconcileEndpoints` function may add endpoint back which was just be deleted in `RemoveEndpoints` function(by update method) , because `ReconcileEndpoints` executed periodically.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/65757763/225651257-523f5cff-ced1-4acf-806b-3d4256c3352d.png)

I might be able to express my point better with this timing diagram. Finally we could still get an valid endpoint If all the event follow the timeline in the diagram, even though this is a small probability event and it will be reconciled in next period by `ReconcileEndpoints`.
Please correct me if I'm wrong. Thank you for your time and patience! @aojea

I see your point and you are right, we should fix `doReconcile` and make it thread safe to avoid possible races.

> Finally we could still get an valid endpoint If all the event follow the timeline in the diagram, even though this is a small probability event and it will be reconciled in next period by ReconcileEndpoints.

However, this can always happen if the callers make a bad use of the methods, ReconcileEndpoints() create endpoints and RemoveEndpoints() remove them, we can only make their use more predictable

The other problem is that we don't handle termination on `doReconcile`that is what the bool will do
FYI: I've opened https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/118777 which I think is related to the fix for this issue.

title: Deleting pods that mount volumes from missing config-maps/secrets causes an abnormal deletion time.
body:
### What happened?

If you create a pod that mounts a volume from a secret or a config-map and then you delete that pod, it takes an abnormally long time to delete the pod.  



### What did you expect to happen?

I would expect a similar time for deletion from a successful case as an unsuccesful case.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

If you have the following yaml:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: config-map-mount
spec:
  containers:
    - name: test-container
      image: registry.k8s.io/busybox
      command: [ "sleep", "100" ]
      volumeMounts:
      - mountPath: /clusters-config
        name: clusters-config-volume
  volumes:
    - configMap:
        name: clusters-config-file
      name: clusters-config-volume
```
And you create it with no config-map and delete the pod it takes around 60-75 seconds to delete the pod.  

If you create that config-map/secret it only takes a few seconds to delete the pod.  

Secret example:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: secret-example-pod
spec:
  containers:
    - name: secret-test-container

title: kubelet issues when LocalStorageCapacityIsolationFSQuotaMonitoring is enabled
body:
### What happened?

1. When the flag is enabled quota setup fails on subsequent invocations

Each time quota is applied on a volume, a new random UUID for the pod is generated and this UUID is compared with the previous stored one internally. If it doesn't match then the whole process stops and an error is returned.

2. ConfigMaps and secrets volume update fail and it floods the cluster with error events

ConfigMaps and secrets use emptyDir volumes which try to reapply quotas on every invocation. Since quota setup fails on subsequent invocations an error is logged each time and the process of updating the payloads is stopped. This happens frequently and it floods the cluster with error messages.

```
kube-system   68s         Warning   FailedMount               pod/kube-proxy-nmmnq                                                (combined from similar events): MountVolume.SetUp failed for volume "kube-proxy" : requesting quota on existing directory /mnt/kubelet/pods/e9f869de-fdf4-4728-a969-34abdaf00683/volumes/kubernetes.io~configmap/kube-proxy but different pod f61ddb8b-82cf-480c-910c-9adbcc643bb2 4e06badc-1093-4076-a127-267aa27ebd46
```

3. After kubelet restarts trying to apply quota fails because the folder already has a quota project id associated with it.

```
monitoring    11m         Warning   FailedMount               pod/prometheus-monitoring-kube-prometheus-prometheus-0              MountVolume.SetUp failed for volume "config-out" : assign quota FAILED createProjectID /mnt/kubelet/pods/ea2780a5-66bb-435c-9395-bf3609839123/volumes/kubernetes.io~empty-dir/config-out 0 failed attempt to reassign project ID for /mnt/kubelet/pods/ea2780a5-66bb-435c-9395-bf3609839123/volumes/kubernetes.io~empty-dir/config-out
```

Similar issues: #114506, #112081

title: A potential issue in the node_affinity
body:
### What happened?

While I was reading the [`node_affinity.go` ](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/nodeaffinity/node_affinity.go)plugin source code in the scheduler, I found there may potentially exist a logic issue in the PreFilter(). 

As from the [document](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/assign-pod-node/#node-affinity) (as well as from [line 125-129](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/nodeaffinity/node_affinity.go#L125) in node_affinity.go), the terms are ORed. However, I found that in [line 132-134](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/nodeaffinity/node_affinity.go#L132), if one term found no matching node, it will return and report `UnschedulableAndUnresolvable`, which makes the logic become ANDed.  Following is the code in line 132-134:
```
if len(termNodeNames) == 0 {
	return nil, framework.NewStatus(framework.UnschedulableAndUnresolvable, errReasonConflict)
}
```

Is this an actual logic issue or if I understand something wrong? 

### What did you expect to happen?

This logic of this code block (line 132-134) may be moved outside this for-loop, and test if the`len(nodeNames)` is 0 instead. 


### Kubernetes version

The master branch

You can have multiple affinity rules, and for each rule you calculate which nodes are following that rule (eq. ``termNodeNames``). You actually do intersection of all ``termNodeNames`` from each termNodeNames and for those you then calculate a score on which you will base your scheduling. So ``termNodeNames`` has  to be in a for loop. The reason for line from 132-134 is simple, because you are using intersection and if one of your set is empty, you can stop the calculation and said that result is empty set. 
But I have to agree that word union is misleading ( because of the ANDing). But again, maybe I am wrong also.

A quote from the document pasted by OP:
> If you specify multiple terms in `nodeSelectorTerm`s associated with `nodeAffinity` types, then the Pod can be scheduled onto a node if one of the specified terms can be satisfied (terms are ORed).

So it shouldn't be intersections.

And unions are the dual of intersections; a correct implementation of them should mean OR.

From [slack](https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C09QYUH5W/p1672832735009399?thread_ts=1672822866.185199&cid=C09QYUH5W):

> loadBalancerIP is assigned to the physical interface (eno1). It accepts traffic from another network there and I use metallb in L2 mode for that. From what I can see, in the dummy interface I have all external addresses used as loadBalancerIP and they are excluded from listening to NodePort - it is as you mentioned

This is not a valid setup. A virtual IP (VIP), like the loadBalancerIP, _must not_ be assigned to a physical interface.

The reason to assign a VIP to a physical interface would be to attract traffic with L2 mechanisms, ARP for IPv4 and neighbor discovery for IPv6, but this way is flawed for several reasons. That's why you use metallb in L2 mode instead. Metallb in L2 mode answers L2 requests _without_ assigning the VIP to any interface.
When you send traffic to a nodePort, the destination address should be a node address, _not_ a loadBalancerIP.

There is however a change in the implementation (I will try to find the PR) in the way the nodePort addresses are computed. This is how i should be;
```
nodePort addresses = addresses on all node interface excluding link-local and loopback and all addresses on kube-ipvs0
```
On `kube-ipvs0` all clusterIP, loadBalancerIP and externalIPs are assigned. So the current implementation is correct.

What I suspect that pre v1.23 K8s did this wrong by adding _all_ addresses on interfaces except kube-ipvs0 (including loopback which would not work).

> This is not a valid setup. A virtual IP (VIP), like the loadBalancerIP, must not be assigned to a physical interface.
The reason to assign a VIP to a physical interface would be to attract traffic with L2 mechanisms, ARP for IPv4 and neighbor discovery for IPv6, but this way is flawed for several reasons. That's why you use metallb in L2 mode instead. Metallb in L2 mode answers L2 requests without assigning the VIP to any interface.

These loadBalancerIP addresses are just the external IP of my nodes, which I use in metallb as an available pool for service(loadbalancer). Provider automatically assigns this address to the physical interface as a lease, I don't really have the option of a different setup at the moment.

> When you send traffic to a nodePort, the destination address should be a node address, not a loadBalancerIP.

Ye, I know. In my case the public IP address pool for node and loadBalancerIP addresses are the same

> These loadBalancerIP addresses are just the external IP of my nodes

So, the loadBalancerIPs assigned by metallb is actually the real addresses of your K8s nodes?

> So, the loadBalancerIPs assigned by metallb is actually the real addresses of your K8s nodes?

Yes, these are public IP addresses (each node has its own), which I use as an entry point for some services(loadbalancer)
but I also have an external loadbalancer that targets nodePort. To eliminate SPoF, it directs traffic to the service (NodePort), which has been listening on all nodes so far, regardless of IP assignment to another service
I will try to test it with iptables, but I use ipvs because of specific services, so I can use the load balancing algorithm - least connection... this method won't solve my problem :(
Found the PR https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/101429

Why do you need nodePorts services at all? Can't you use only loadBalancer?

NodePort is mainly intended to be used by and external load-balancer, i.e. like in AWS, but when you manage your own cluster you usually don't have an external loadBalancer so use only loadBalancerIPs makes sense. We do that, and even [disable nodePort allocation](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/service/#load-balancer-nodeport-allocation).

> ~Why do you need nodePorts services at all? Can't you use only loadBalancer?~

Scratch that! In your case where the node addresses are the external addresses you should use NodePort _only_.

If you use your node addresses as loadBalancerIP you will hit this PR https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/108460 when you upgrade to later K8s versions. It inserts a blocking rule in the INPUT chain for loadBalancerIPs.

## WARNING
This will block input to your node if loadBalancerIP==nodeIP.
I understand, thanks for the info. In my case it's a breaking change and I will have to migrate some services to NodePort before kubernetes upgrade on prod environment.

> @adr-xyt Thanks for explaining. I understand your setup now, . I am unsure if it's supposed to work, so I have to ask. Have you tested proxy-mode=iptables? It may work, but I wouldn't be suprised if it doesn't.

@uablrek 

with proxy-mode=iptables, everything started working, node is listening on nodePort and I can get to loadBalancerIP, I cleared the rules `kube-proxy --cleanup` on each node, just to be sure
However this is not a solution for me, I need the lc algorithm from ipvs

> I will have to migrate some services to NodePort before kubernetes upgrade on prod environment.

Port 31010 used in the LoadBakancer service example is within the default NodePort range. I think it can be converted to a NodePort service without affecting external users. Or is 31010 just an example? Or are there other reasons for type:LoadBalancer?
/area ipvs

> Port 31010 used in the LoadBakancer service example is within the default NodePort range. I think it can be converted to a NodePort service without affecting external users. Or is 31010 just an example? Or are there other reasons for type:LoadBalancer?

This is just an example, I won't have much trouble with the migration. At most, I will divide the available lease of IP addresses into smaller pools, for NodePort / Loadblancer services. 
I think I already know everything and there should be no more surprises. 
Thanks for the information and your time!

It is a little "unusal" to use the host IP as the LB IP, but it's unfortunate that we broke something that used to work.  https://www.hyrumslaw.com/

Lars, is there any path back to "working" that doesn't lose the protections in that linked PR?

I could easily see iptables *also* breaking this..

To not exclude loadBalancerIPs (and ecternalIPs) when they are on a physical interface is not hard, but messes up the nice set-operation.

The access protection in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/108460 It should basically not be there if the any loadBalancerIPs (and ecternalIPs) is also on aphysical interface. Can be done, but may be messy.

/triage accepted

Even though this issue is accepted, it's still under investigation.

I will check the code if the old bevaivor can be restored in a fairly simple way. But there is a problem with back-port. If I make a PR now it will be in v1.26.x or v1.27 but the function was broken in v1.23 so a fix should really be back-ported all the way back.

I would prefer to document that a real address on an interface on the node can't be used as a virtual address, like loadBalancerIP or externalIP.

Just wanted to chime in and say that I've also encountered this issue... very grateful to find the discussion and looking forward to a solution.  Thank you all!

Also just to share, I've tried the following 3 workarounds and they all work in my case:
- Switching to iptables mode.  It works I think because the iptables NAT rule refers to the hostname as the destination, which gets resolved to the public node IP.
- Disable IPv6 on my OS.  This works too as it makes the code fall back to the single stack mode, which grabs the node IP also from looking up the hostname.
- Explicitly configure the `nodePortAddresses` field in the kube proxy config, that overrides the default get local addresses.

@adr-xyt I backed down to K8s v1.22.4 and I can't get it to work unless you have the master outside the cluster (i.e. not a node), or have a setup where the external-ip you set as loadBalancerIP is _not_ on the main K8s network, something like; K8s is using the "backend" network, the "external" ips are on the "frontend" network. The reason is when you assign a loadBalancerIP, that address will be assigned to the `kube-ipvs0` interface, even before v1.23. So, on an in-cluster master node you will see something like; ``` vm-001 ~ # ip addr show dev kube-ipvs0 15: kube-ipvs0: mtu 1500 qdisc noop state DOWN group default link/ether 1a:8d:7f:b9:0a:95 brd ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff inet 12.0.0.1/32 scope global kube-ipvs0 valid_lft forever preferred_lft forever inet 12.0.253.214/32 scope global kube-ipvs0 valid_lft forever preferred_lft forever inet 12.0.117.25/32 scope global kube-ipvs0 valid_lft forever preferred_lft forever inet 192.168.1.2/32 scope global kube-ipvs0 ``` The `192.168.1.2` address is the loadBalancerIP and is also the node-address of another node in the cluster, "vm-002". When the master receives "normal" packets from "vm-002" they will have src=192.168.1.2 but since that address is assigned to a local interface on the master the packets will be discarded as [martians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martian_packet) or spoofed packets. The result is that "vm-002" (e.g. `kubelet` on that node) loses contact with the master; ``` vm-002 ~ # kubectl version Client Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"22", GitVersion:"v1.22.4", GitCommit:"b695d79d4f967c403a96986f1750a35eb75e75f1", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2021-11-17T15:48:33Z", GoVersion:"go1.16.10", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/amd64"} Unable to connect to the server: dial tcp 192.168.1.1:6443: connect: no route to host ```
I discovered this when testing PR https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/115019. I think I can restore the pre v1.23 behavior now, but I suffer from the problem described above.
@chlam4 I don't think your problem is precisely the same. To disable ipv6 or set nodePortAddresses can't really be used as work-arounds for this issue.

@chlam4 You are right. To explicitly set `nodePortAddresses` in the kube-proxy config works as a work-around.

Still the loadBalancerIP (which is also an address on a node) can't be used by the main k8s network, or the master must not be a node in the cluster as described in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/114815#issuecomment-1382090138. And...

## Warning

This will work up to and including K8s v1.25.x, but **_NOT v1.26.0!_** I haven't checked yet but I think it's because of https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/108460.

Since the loadBalancerIP that is owned by a node is assigned to `kube-ipvs0` on _other_ nodes you must stop those other nodes from responding to ARP. For example with:
```
sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.all.arp_ignore=1
```

From my perspective, this is not a big [problem](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/114815#issuecomment-1382090138), I have the whole architecture implemented in separate networks. I think it's worth adding this information somewhere in the documentation.

@uablrek Thank you so much for the response, epesically the info about v1.26.  We'll check it out for sure and will report back.  Our node port use case is for single-node deployments only, so luckily there are no other nodes.

nodes.title: Allow node addresses to be used as loadBalancer addresses for proxy-mode=ipvs
nodes.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug
/sig network
/area kube-proxy
/area ipvs

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

To use node-addresses as loadBalancerIP works with proxy-mode=iptables and did work before K8s v1.23 for proxy-mode=ipvs.

A problem with kernel versions and netlink fixed in PR https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/101429 caused the problem reported in #114815. The addresses assigned for NodePort became `AllAddresses - addresses(kube-ipvs0)`, but the the node-address is a loadBalancerIP it is assigned (also) to kube-ipvs0 and is thus excluded.

The security fix in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/108460 prevents access to ports on the node (like ssh) to be accesible via loadBalancerIPs and clusterIPs, but if a loadBalancerIPs is also a node-ip, then **access to the node will be blocked**.

Both these problems must be taken care of in this PR.


#### Which issue(s) this PR fixes:

Fixes #114815, #117613

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

**NOTE** I am splitting this PR into one for the cleanup https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/115073 and will re-build this PR on top of that.



#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
Fixes a 1.26 regression in kube-proxy ipvs mode
```

title: Job back-offs get reset on controller-manager restart
body:
### What happened?

Exponential back-off kicks in when a pod fails. The back-off logic is offloaded to the in-memory `workqueue` data structure. On controller-manager restarts, the information in the `workqueue` is lost. So, the back-off information is lost and the back-off gets calculated as if the job is a new one.

### What did you expect to happen?

The pods to be created with correct back-offs even when the controller-manager restarts

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Start a job that always fail
2. Let the job fail till we see a visible back-off
3. Stop the controller-manager container
4. New pod gets scheduled immediately after controller-manager restart irrespective of the previously computed back-off

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

There is a more immediate problem for me:
All job syncs are tied to the workqueue delays. We should just be delaying pod creation, but not job status updates. This is specially important when the job hits the `backoffLimit`. We would wait X seconds before declaring the Job as failed, even though it could be done immediately.

I think the solution is somewhat simple: keep track of the elapsed time within the sync, instead of the workqueue and restrict pod creation specifically. The time should be measured based on the Pod status, to be resilient to restarts. But even if we can't do that immediately, just tracking in memory shouldn't be too bad to start.

body:
### What happened?

Hello, I've recently been testing the reliability of storage for k8s **v1.25.0.** A strange phenomenon occurs occasionally during the test: the volume cannot be detached after the PVC and pod are deleted(the reclaimPolicy of pv is delete）.
So I first went to check the corresponding `pv` and `volumeAttachment` objects and found that they both existed. Then I checked the kube-controllerManager and kubelet logs and found that kubelet logs kept printing:

`I1125 10:28:42.931263 3908451 reconciler.go:389] "Starting operationExecutor.UnmountDevice for volume \"pvc-1a4bcff1-f11d-456c-b91a-1aaa5c3ea5db\" (UniqueName: \"kubernetes.io/csi/xxx^f2ee34c4-f297-49cb-8730-4442ceb1df4f\") on node \"192.168.x.x\" "`

it is so wired !

I think this is again a TOCTOU bug in unmountDetachDevices.

The Unmount operation is [async](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/volume/util/nestedpendingoperations/nestedpendingoperations.go#L185-L191), thus the `DeviceMount` state may not be set as `Notmounted` before next reconcile, so it is possible that unmountDevice operation performed multiple times. So the root cause of this issue is that [getDriverAndVolNameFromDeviceMountPath](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/volume/csi/csi_attacher.go#L691-L692) got wrong PV name, since  https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/107065 changed global mount path.

title: [Winkernel Proxier] No ingress load balancer rules with endpoints to support load balancing when all the endpoints are terminating
body:
### What happened?

HNS requires the Load Balancing Policy to be configured to identify the traffic destined to a cloud providers Load Balancer IP (VIP) and forward it to the distributed Load Balancer running in VFP on the node. Windows Kube-proxy ignores the terminating endpoints and strictly creates a HNS Load Balancer policy only for "Ready" pods that are not terminating. This creates a problem when all the PODs serving as backends for a Service are terminating. The traffic for active connections is not delivered to the Distributed LoadBalancer and dropped on the Windows node.

### What did you expect to happen?

Windows Kube-proxy/HNS should handle the terminating endpoints correctly to minimize the network traffic loss.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a Service of Type LoadBalancer with exactly one POD as a backend.
2. Establish a long running TCP connection from an external Client to the Service.
3. Scale the deployment to delete the POD.
4. The active connection is immediately broken. A prestop hook handler configured on the POD will not get a chance to gracefully terminate the connection.

### Kubernetes version

1.24.0 and above

### Cloud provider

Azure Kubernetes Service

### OS version

Windows Server 2019, Windows Server 2022

title: coreDNS image reports the wrong architecture
body:
### What happened?

The docker images for linux/arm64 wrongly report their architecture as amd64. This issue affects at least the `v1.8.6` and `v1.9.3` of the coredns images.


### What did you expect to happen?

Expected the arm64 version of the image to correctly report its architecture as arm64.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

## 1) Pull the image, specifying the linux/arm64 platform.
```bash
> docker pull --platform linux/arm64 registry.k8s.io/coredns/coredns:v1.8.6

v1.8.6: Pulling from coredns/coredns
Digest: sha256:5b6ec0d6de9baaf3e92d0f66cd96a25b9edbce8716f5f15dcd1a616b3abd590e
Status: Image is up to date for registry.k8s.io/coredns/coredns:v1.8.6
registry.k8s.io/coredns/coredns:v1.8.6
```

## 2) Inspect the image for the digest linked to the specified platform.
```bash
> docker inspect -f '{{.Architecture}}' registry.k8s.io/coredns/coredns:v1.8.6@sha256:5b6ec0d6de9baaf3e92d0f66cd96a25b9edbce8716f5f15dcd1a616b3abd590e

amd64
```

The above images is not showing the correct architecture. 

Note that this issue is sometimes silent when using MacOS as the platform does support running amd64 images. e.g. `kind` can create a working cluster even with the wrong image arch. However, using e.g. `kind load` will fail as there is an architecture check when this command is run.

Ah, OK, this might be related to runc, since the error comes from runc code. Having said that, I am not aware of any bugs in runc 1.1.4 that can result in this error.

Now, what runc does is it sends the `StopUnit` command to systemd (this is the same thing that happens when you issue `systemctl stop $UNIT`) and waits for up to 30 seconds for systemd to respond. Generally, 30s it is enough for systemd to remove the unit (or report an error), but it does not happen in this case and so the timeout is hit.

What this means, practically, is systemd is currently having some major issues and is not very responsive. I would start to debug this particular issue by reproducing it and when looking into system logs (journalctl) to see what's going on. Checking how systemd copes in would make sense, too.

@AndrewSav this was because you switched from cgroups v1 (ubuntu 20 default) to v2 ( Ubuntu 22 default).
